name: Reading Financial Statements
description: How the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement fit together.
intro: Every finance and consulting interview eventually touches the three financial statements, the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, because they are how a business actually gets described in numbers. This deck is built for someone who has never opened a company’s annual report: it walks through what each statement shows, why they exist as three separate documents instead of one, and how a single transaction ripples across all three. By the end, you should be able to hear "walk me through the financial statements" and actually enjoy answering it.

cards.q: You're staffed on the Kestrel Components sale process, and the VP asks you to walk the client's newly hired CFO through how the three financial statements tie together before the first management presentation. What do you say?
cards.takeaway: Net income is the thread that stitches the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement together.
cards.a: You'd start with the income statement, which shows profitability over a period: revenue minus expenses equals net income. Then the balance sheet, a snapshot of what the company owns and owes at one specific moment, assets, liabilities, and equity. Then the cash flow statement, which tracks how cash actually moved during that same period. Net income is what ties them together: it flows into the cash flow statement's starting line and into retained earnings on the balance sheet.

cards.q: What’s the key difference between the balance sheet and the income statement in terms of time?
cards.takeaway: The income statement covers a stretch of time; the balance sheet freezes one exact moment.
cards.a: The income statement covers a period, a quarter or a year, showing what happened over that stretch. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one exact moment, showing what the company owns and owes as of that date. Think of it like the difference between a video and a photo: one captures a stretch of activity, the other captures a single instant.

cards.q: The Windmere Foods deal has a working capital adjustment built into the purchase agreement, and your associate asks you to explain what working capital actually measures before you build the mechanism into the model. What do you tell them?
cards.takeaway: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, a quick read on short-term liquidity.
cards.a: Working capital measures how easily a company can cover its near-term obligations: current assets minus current liabilities. A positive number means the company has enough short-term assets, cash, receivables, inventory, to meet what it owes in the near future. A shrinking or negative figure is exactly the kind of thing diligence flags as an early warning sign of cash flow trouble ahead, and it's why working capital pegs and adjustments show up in almost every purchase agreement.

cards.q: During diligence on the Talbrook Industries acquisition, the target's net income looks strong but its cash balance keeps falling. Your associate asks you to explain why the two numbers can diverge in the same period.
cards.takeaway: Net income books revenue the moment it's earned; cash flow only counts money that's actually landed.
cards.a: Net income includes non-cash items like depreciation, and under accrual accounting it counts revenue as soon as it's earned, not when the cash actually arrives. Cash flow only counts money that has physically moved. That's exactly how a target can show a healthy profit on paper while its cash balance falls, if customers haven't paid yet or cash is tied up sitting in inventory, which is precisely the kind of gap diligence is meant to catch.

cards.q: What are the three sections of the cash flow statement?
cards.takeaway: Operating, investing, and financing activities add up to explain exactly why cash changed.
cards.a: Operating activities capture cash generated or used by the core business. Investing activities cover cash spent on or received from things like equipment or acquisitions. Financing activities capture cash from debt, equity raises, dividends, or buybacks. Add all three together in the model and you get the full explanation for why the cash balance changed over the period.

cards.q: How does depreciation affect the income statement differently than the cash flow statement?
cards.takeaway: Depreciation cuts net income as an expense, then gets added straight back on the cash flow statement.
cards.a: Depreciation reduces net income on the income statement because it's recorded as an expense, even though no cash actually leaves the business that period. On the cash flow statement, it gets added back in the operating section, since that statement's whole job is to reflect real cash movement, not accounting expense, which is exactly the line the deal team double-checks first when a cash flow build doesn't tie out.

cards.q: What is the accounting equation?
cards.takeaway: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity, everything owned was funded by debt or by owners.
cards.a: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Everything a company owns, its assets, was funded either by borrowing (liabilities) or by owners' investment and retained profit (equity). The balance sheet has to balance to this equation at all times, which is exactly where its name comes from.

cards.q: What does accrual accounting mean, and how is it different from cash accounting?
cards.takeaway: Accrual accounting counts revenue when it's earned, not when the cash actually shows up.
cards.a: Accrual accounting records revenue when it's earned and expenses when they're incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands, so a sale made on credit counts as revenue immediately. Cash accounting only records a transaction once cash physically moves. Nearly every company you'll model uses accrual accounting, because it matches revenue to the period it was actually generated in, giving a truer picture of performance than the cash sitting in the bank that day.

cards.q: The Overton Digital pitch materials quote an EV/EBITDA multiple, and the analyst next to you asks what EBITDA actually captures before it goes into the comp set. What do you tell them?
cards.takeaway: EBITDA adds interest, taxes, and D&A back to net income to isolate pure operating performance.
cards.a: EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, essentially operating profit before the effects of financing decisions and non-cash accounting charges. It shows up everywhere in comps and LBO models because it lets you compare operating performance across companies with different capital structures or tax situations, stripping those differences away to leave the core business result.

name: Valuation Basics
description: DCF, comps, and the multiples analysts actually use.
intro: Valuation is the skill of putting a number on what a company or investment is actually worth, and it is one of the most commonly tested topics in finance interviews, from "walk me through a DCF" to "how would you value this company." This deck introduces the core methods, discounted cash flow, comparable companies, and the multiples analysts lean on, in plain language first, then in the more technical form interviewers expect. No prior valuation experience assumed, just a willingness to think in terms of cash flow and comparison.

cards.q: Your VP asks you to talk her through the DCF tab before tomorrow's client call: why discount every year of projected free cash flow back to today instead of just adding the numbers up? What is a DCF actually doing?
cards.takeaway: A DCF says a company is worth all the cash it will ever generate, brought back to today's dollars.
cards.a: You forecast the company's free cash flow for the next several years, then discount each year back to present value using a discount rate (usually WACC), since a dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today: it carries risk, and that same dollar could be earning a return elsewhere. Add those discounted years together, plus a terminal value for everything beyond the forecast window, and that sum is what lands in the model as today's value.

cards.q: Your MD asks you to sanity-check the WACC on the Ferrow Retail LBO model before the 9am call. What is WACC actually representing, and why does it belong in the discount rate?
cards.takeaway: WACC is the blended cost of a company's money, part debt, part equity.
cards.a: Every company funds itself with some mix of debt and equity, and each has a cost: debt costs interest (though it's tax-deductible, making it effectively cheaper than its stated rate), equity costs the return shareholders expect. WACC blends those two costs, weighted by how much of each the company actually uses. It's used as the discount rate in the model because it represents the minimum return Ferrow's investments need to clear to be worth funding — if the WACC input is off, everything downstream is off with it.

cards.q: What is “terminal value” in a DCF, and why does it get so much scrutiny in a model review?
cards.takeaway: Terminal value covers everything a business earns after the forecast period ends.
cards.a: A DCF only forecasts explicitly for about 5–10 years, but the company is assumed to keep operating indefinitely beyond that. Terminal value estimates all of that remaining future in one lump sum, discounted back to today just like any other cash flow. It's typically the single largest piece of a DCF's total value — which is exactly why an MD will push hard on the assumptions behind it, a long-run growth rate or an exit multiple, before a number goes in front of a client.

cards.q: What is comparable company analysis (“comps”), and why do bankers reach for it before running a full DCF?
cards.takeaway: Comps value a company by comparing it to similar public companies' current pricing.
cards.a: Instead of building a value from scratch like a DCF does, comps anchor to what the market is already paying for similar businesses, typically using a ratio like EV/EBITDA or P/E, then apply that same multiple to the company being valued. It's a relative valuation method: quicker to turn around for a pitch book than a DCF, and it reflects real market sentiment, for better or worse.

cards.q: A client asks why your team is quoting Halsey Aerospace's value on an EV/EBITDA basis instead of just comparing share prices. What does EV/EBITDA measure, and why use enterprise value instead of market cap?
cards.takeaway: EV/EBITDA compares total company value to operating earnings, ignoring how the company is financed.
cards.a: Enterprise value is used instead of market cap because it also accounts for debt and cash, making it possible to compare companies fairly even when they have very different capital structures: market cap alone ignores how much of the business is funded by debt. EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) strips out financing and accounting choices, so you're comparing pure operating performance, which is exactly why the multiple travels well across a set of comps.

cards.q: Marlstone Capital is evaluating a buyout of Ferrow Retail and wants to know the total price tag versus what's left for shareholders. What's the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
cards.takeaway: Enterprise value is the whole business; equity value is just the shareholders' slice.
cards.a: Enterprise value represents the value of the whole business — what Marlstone would need to pay to acquire Ferrow outright, including taking on its debt and stripping out its cash. Equity value is just the value belonging to shareholders (what market cap represents). The bridge between them: enterprise value = equity value + debt − cash.

cards.q: What is a P/E ratio, and what does a high P/E typically signal to a banker sizing up a target?
cards.takeaway: P/E shows how much investors pay today for each dollar the company currently earns.
cards.a: The price-to-earnings ratio divides a company's share price by its earnings per share. A high P/E usually signals that the market expects strong future earnings growth, since investors are willing to pay more today for the same current profit; it can also simply mean the target is overvalued relative to its fundamentals, so P/E alone doesn't tell you which story is true.

cards.q: Your VP asks why the precedent transaction multiples you pulled for the Bramwell & Co. pitch are running higher than the trading comps for the same sector. What is precedent transactions analysis, and how does it differ from comps?
cards.takeaway: Precedent transactions value a company using prices actually paid in past M&A deals.
cards.a: Unlike comps, which look at how similar companies trade on public markets day-to-day, this method looks at what acquirers have actually paid to buy similar businesses outright. Because acquisitions usually include a control premium (extra paid to gain control of the company), precedent transaction multiples tend to run higher than trading comps — which is exactly the gap your VP is asking about.

cards.q: Before the Corrigan Foods pitch book goes to print, your MD asks why the valuation page shows a range instead of one clean number. Why does a valuation usually get presented as a range (a “football field”) rather than a single number?
cards.takeaway: A valuation range, not one number, because every method rests on assumptions that can shift.
cards.a: Growth rates, discount rates, which comps are truly comparable: small changes in any of these assumptions can shift the output meaningfully. Presenting a range across multiple methods (DCF, comps, precedent transactions) is more honest about that uncertainty than putting one falsely precise number in front of a client.

name: Excel for Financial Modeling
description: The modeling habits and shortcuts a first-year analyst is expected to know cold.
intro: Excel is the quiet backbone of every IB analyst seat, and interviewers use it as a proxy for whether you can actually build and check a model under time pressure, not just talk about one. This deck covers the linking discipline, formatting conventions, and modeling habits that come up constantly: keeping a 3-statement model tied together, handling circular references cleanly, building sensitivity tables, and the small checks that separate a clean model from a fragile one. If you've mostly used Excel for basic formulas so far, start here.

cards.q: Why do banker-built models color hardcoded inputs blue and formulas black, and what does a green cell usually mean?
cards.takeaway: Color-coding cells by type lets anyone audit a model's logic at a glance, without opening the formula bar.
cards.a: On the Street, font color is a substitute for documentation: blue marks a hardcoded input typed directly into the cell, black marks a formula that calculates from other cells, and green marks a link pulling in a value from another worksheet or workbook. That convention lets anyone glance at a tab and instantly separate the assumptions someone is allowed to change from the calculations that shouldn't be touched by hand. Breaking it, a blue cell that's secretly a formula, or a formula colored blue, is one of the fastest ways to look sloppy in front of an MD, because it hides where the model's real control panel is.

cards.q: Why do IB analysts build models almost entirely with the keyboard, and which shortcuts should you know cold?
cards.takeaway: Mouse-free navigation is faster and steadier, and interviewers watch for it directly in a live Excel test.
cards.a: Analysts spend most of the workweek inside Excel, so a second saved on every cell-to-cell move compounds fast, and reaching for the mouse breaks the train of thought while building a formula. Interviewers watch how a candidate moves around the sheet almost as closely as whether the final number is right, because mouse-heavy navigation is a tell for inexperience. Know cold: Ctrl+Arrow to jump to the edge of a data block, Ctrl+Shift+Arrow to select to that edge, F4 to cycle a reference between relative and absolute, Ctrl+Alt+V for Paste Special, and Ctrl+` to toggle formula view. These aren't optional polish, they're assumed baseline fluency by the time you're in the room.

cards.q: Your associate flags that changing the D&A assumption in your Ferrow Retail model doesn't move the ending cash balance. What's the likely problem?
cards.takeaway: In a properly linked model, one input change ripples through all three statements to the cash balance.
cards.a: In a correctly built model, D&A hits the income statement, reducing pre-tax income and taxes, flows into the cash flow statement as a non-cash add-back, and reduces the PP&E balance on the balance sheet; the cash flow statement's ending cash then becomes the balance sheet's cash line. If changing D&A doesn't move ending cash, a link is broken somewhere in that chain, most often the CFS add-back is hardcoded instead of pulling from the income statement, or the balance sheet's cash cell isn't actually pointing at the CFS's ending-cash line. Trace it cell by cell with Ctrl+[ to find precedents rather than guessing, confirming each statement genuinely pulls live from the one before it.

cards.q: While building the debt schedule for the Bramwell & Co. LBO, Excel throws a circular reference warning. Why did that happen, and how do you handle it?
cards.takeaway: Interest expense depending on a debt balance that depends on interest expense is a real, expected circularity.
cards.a: A debt schedule is circular by construction: interest expense on the income statement reduces net income and the cash available for debt paydown, but the beginning debt balance used to calculate that same interest expense depends on how much debt was already paid down, which depends on that cash flow. Excel can't resolve a loop like that on its own and throws a circular reference warning, or returns zeros and errors. The fix is to turn on iterative calculation (File > Options > Formulas > Enable iterative calculation) so Excel recalculates the loop until it converges, and to build in a circularity breaker switch, a cell or checkbox that can force interest expense to zero, so an unrelated error elsewhere doesn't spin the whole model into cascading #REF or #VALUE errors.

cards.q: Your MD wants a table showing the Bramwell & Co. LBO's exit IRR across a range of exit multiples and entry leverage levels. What Excel feature builds this in one shot?
cards.takeaway: A two-variable data table recalculates one output across every combination of two input ranges automatically.
cards.a: Excel's Data Table, under What-If Analysis, recalculates a single output formula across every combination of two input ranges without you writing a formula in each cell. You lay out a grid with one variable's values down the left column (say, exit multiples), the other across the top row (leverage levels), put the output formula, like IRR, in the top-left corner cell, then select the whole grid and tell Excel which cell each axis should feed as the row input and column input. Excel substitutes each combination in turn and fills the grid, which is also why large data tables can noticeably slow down recalculation. It's the standard way to hand an MD a range of outcomes instead of a single point estimate.

cards.q: How would you build a clean scenario toggle in a model, say switching between a Base Case and Downside Case set of assumptions, without breaking anything downstream?
cards.takeaway: A single toggle cell, driven by one dropdown, should be the only thing every downstream formula reads.
cards.a: The clean pattern is one dedicated toggle cell, built with a data validation dropdown listing something like "Base" and "Downside," or a simple 1/0 cell tied to a checkbox. Every assumption in the model that has more than one scenario version should be written as something like =CHOOSE($B$2,BaseValue,DownsideValue) or =IF($B$2="Base",BaseValue,DownsideValue), reading that same single toggle, so flipping the dropdown once cascades through the entire model instantly. The discipline is that no downstream formula ever hardcodes its own scenario choice; everything points back to the one switch, so there's exactly one cell to check to know which case the model is currently showing.

cards.q: You need to pull a comp company's EV/EBITDA multiple from a Comps tab into your output page, but the row order won't stay fixed as companies get added or re-sorted. What's the safer approach?
cards.takeaway: INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP survives inserted rows and reordering; a hardcoded row reference does not.
cards.a: Use INDEX/MATCH, or in modern Excel, XLOOKUP, rather than pointing directly at a specific row, because comps lists get re-sorted, re-ranked, or have companies added mid-deal. MATCH, or XLOOKUP's lookup argument, finds the row position of the company name, and INDEX, or XLOOKUP's return array, pulls the multiple from that row in whichever column you choose, so the formula still finds the right value even after the list changes shape. XLOOKUP is the newer single-function version of the same idea, defaults to an exact match, and can search in either direction, but INDEX/MATCH is still worth knowing cold since not every bank's template or Excel version has XLOOKUP available.

cards.q: Before sending your Bramwell & Co. LBO model to the MD, how do you sanity-check that it isn't secretly broken?
cards.takeaway: A visible balance check and error traps catch a broken model before your MD does.
cards.a: Every balance sheet should carry a check row, typically =Total Assets - Total Liabilities and Equity, wrapped in something like =IF(ROUND(Assets-Liabilities,0)=0,"OK","ERROR") so it's impossible to miss the moment the sheet stops balancing. Beyond that, wrap fragile formulas, lookups, divisions, anything that depends on an input existing, in IFERROR so a missing value produces a visible flag instead of a #N/A or #DIV/0! buried in a cell nobody's looking at, and scan the model with Ctrl+` or Excel's formula-auditing tools before circulating it. The habit that actually matters in an interview is naming this discipline unprompted: a model that runs without errors but was never checked for balance is not considered done on the Street.

cards.q: You've pulled comps output for Ferrow Retail into a summary page using live formulas, and now need to send a static snapshot to the deal team that won't change later. What's the move?
cards.takeaway: Paste Special > Values converts live formulas into fixed numbers, severing the link to their source cells.
cards.a: Copy the range, then Paste Special (Ctrl+Alt+V, or the classic Alt+E, S, V) and choose "Values" instead of a normal paste, which pastes the calculated result as a static number and strips out the underlying formula along with any link to the source cells or tabs. That's the standard way to freeze a snapshot before sending a model externally, turning a live comps pull into a fixed exhibit that won't silently change if someone edits the source tab later, and it's also the way to break a link when copying data between workbooks so the destination file doesn't stay dependent on a file that might get moved or deleted. It gets used constantly inside a model too, for example hardcoding a final negotiated purchase price so it stops moving every time a live market-data pull updates.

name: Corporate Finance & Investment Basics
description: Time value of money, NPV, IRR, and how companies decide where to put capital.
intro: This deck is about how companies actually decide where to put their money, using ideas like the time value of money, net present value, and internal rate of return. These concepts sound abstract until you realize interviewers use them to test whether you can reason about a decision the way a finance team actually would. Expect a mix of "what does this term mean" and "how would you use it to make a call," both of which come up in real interviews.

cards.q: What is the time value of money, and why does it matter?
cards.takeaway: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can already be earning a return.
cards.a: Money in hand today is worth more than the same amount later, because it can be invested right away to start earning a return, and because inflation and risk chip away at what a future dollar can actually buy. This is the foundational idea behind discounting, NPV, and virtually every valuation method bankers build: you can't compare a dollar today to a dollar in five years, or line up cash flows from different points in a deal timeline, without adjusting for that gap first.

cards.q: You're on the deal team pitching Bramwell & Co., a mid-market packaging manufacturer, on a $40mm plant expansion. Your VP asks you to walk him through what Net Present Value is and how you'd use it to tell the client whether the expansion is worth funding.
cards.takeaway: NPV converts a project's future cash flows into today's dollars and nets out what it cost to get started.
cards.a: NPV takes the expansion's expected future cash flows, discounts each one back to present value using Bramwell's cost of capital, and adds them all up. Then it subtracts the initial $40mm outlay, leaving the net value the project is actually expected to create. The decision rule follows directly: recommend the project if NPV is positive, since it's expected to earn more than the cost of capital, and recommend against it if NPV is negative.

cards.q: You're building the returns page for a leveraged buyout of Ferrow Retail ahead of the investment committee meeting. The senior associate asks you to explain what the IRR line in the model actually represents.
cards.takeaway: IRR is the discount rate that makes a deal's NPV exactly zero, its own break-even return.
cards.a: IRR is the discount rate at which the deal's projected cash flows produce an NPV of exactly zero, so it's essentially the LBO's built-in break-even rate of return. To judge whether the Ferrow Retail deal clears the bar, you'd compare its IRR against the fund's required return, or hurdle rate: if the projected IRR beats that hurdle, the deal is generally worth pursuing.

cards.q: What is the payback period, and what's its main limitation?
cards.takeaway: Payback period tells you how fast you get your money back, but ignores everything after that.
cards.a: The payback period is simply how long it takes for a project's cumulative cash flows to add back up to the initial investment. Its main blind spot is that it ignores the time value of money, treating a dollar in year one the same as a dollar in year four, and it ignores any cash flows after the payback point. Bankers will sometimes use it as a quick sanity-check gut number, but it's usually paired with NPV or IRR rather than used as a stand-alone decision tool.

cards.q: Your MD wants a one-line capital structure summary for Halloway Industrial ahead of tomorrow's board deck: how much of the balance sheet is funded with debt versus equity, and why the mix is worth flagging.
cards.takeaway: Capital structure is just the mix of debt and equity a company uses to fund itself.
cards.a: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity Halloway uses to fund its operations and growth. That mix matters because it shapes the company's cost of capital, risk, and flexibility: debt is generally cheaper and doesn't dilute ownership, but it comes with fixed repayment obligations regardless of how the business performs, while equity carries no repayment obligation but costs more and dilutes existing owners.

cards.q: What is the difference between a bond and a stock, at a basic level?
cards.takeaway: A bond is a loan with a promised repayment; a stock is ownership with no promises either way.
cards.a: A bond is essentially a loan: an investor gives a company or government money, and in return it promises to pay back the principal plus periodic interest (coupons) on a fixed schedule. A stock is different: it represents partial ownership in a company, with no promised repayment at all. Its value simply depends on the company's future performance and however the market chooses to price that, which is exactly why equity and debt sit on opposite ends of the risk-return spectrum in a deal's financing mix.

cards.q: Your MD asks you to sanity-check the WACC on the Corven Aerospace model before the 9am call. Walk him through what "cost of capital" actually means and why it's the number sitting at the center of that check.
cards.takeaway: Cost of capital is the minimum return a company must earn on anything it invests in, or it's destroying value.
cards.a: Cost of capital is the return Corven has to offer to attract funding, whether that's interest paid to lenders (cost of debt) or the return shareholders expect (cost of equity), and it rises with how risky investors perceive the company to be. Think of it as a hurdle rate: any project or investment Corven takes on needs to earn more than this just to be worth doing, which is exactly why a WACC that's out of line with the company's risk profile is worth flagging before it goes in front of the client.

cards.q: What is diversification, and why does it reduce risk?
cards.takeaway: Diversification spreads money across assets that don't all move together, smoothing out the bumps.
cards.a: Diversification means spreading your money across multiple assets whose returns don't move in lockstep, so when one investment dips, others are likely holding steady or gaining, cushioning the blow. Because different assets react differently to the same events, a diversified portfolio typically ends up with lower overall volatility than any single holding inside it.

cards.q: What is the difference between systematic and unsystematic risk?
cards.takeaway: Systematic risk hits the whole market and can't be diversified away; unsystematic risk is company-specific and can.
cards.a: Systematic risk is market-wide, things like interest rate moves or a recession, and it affects nearly every asset at once, so no amount of diversification eliminates it. Unsystematic risk is specific to a single company or industry, like a product recall or a lawsuit, and this is the risk diversification actually protects against: spread your holdings widely enough, and one asset's specific problems just get absorbed by the others. It's also why beta in a WACC calculation only ever measures the systematic piece.

name: Statistics & Data Analysis for Business
description: The core statistical concepts behind sound, defensible business analysis.
intro: Most business and data roles do not expect you to be a statistician, but they do expect you to reason clearly about numbers: what an average actually tells you, when a sample might be misleading, how confident you can really be in a conclusion. This deck focuses on the statistical concepts that come up in business contexts specifically, not abstract math theory, so the framing stays close to how you would actually use it in an interview or on the job. No statistics background required to start.

cards.q: You're advising Ferrow Retail Group on store performance. The regional director's slide says “average weekly revenue across our 40 stores is $84K” — but one flagship store does 5x the volume of any other location. What's the risk in leaning on that number, and how do mean, median, and mode differ?
cards.takeaway: Mean is the average, median is the middle, mode is the most common — skewed data favors the median.
cards.a: The regional director's mean gets pulled upward by that one outlier store, making the “typical” store look stronger than it actually is. Mean adds up every value and divides by the count, median is the middle value once everything's sorted, and mode is whichever value shows up most often. Because the mean gets dragged around by outliers, the median holds steady and gives a better read on what a typical store is actually doing — the same logic applies to skewed data like income or home prices.

cards.takeaway: Standard deviation measures how tightly values cluster around the average — small means consistent, large means volatile.
cards.a: Standard deviation tells you how far values typically stray from the mean. A small standard deviation means the data clusters tightly around the average — consistent, predictable — while a large one means values swing widely in either direction. cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group's CEO points out that stores with an in-store café also have higher electronics sales, and concludes the café is driving people to buy more electronics. What's wrong with that conclusion, and how would you push back?
cards.takeaway: Two variables moving together doesn't mean one causes the other — a hidden third factor might explain both.
cards.a: The CEO is treating a correlation as if it were proven causation. Two variables moving together doesn't mean one causes the other — cafés and strong electronics sales might both simply show up in larger, higher-traffic stores, a hidden third factor driving both. Before recommending the client roll out cafés chain-wide, you'd want to isolate that store-size effect or run a controlled test, since proving causation usually takes an experiment or careful statistical work, not just an observed pattern.

cards.q: What is a p-value, in plain terms?
cards.takeaway: A p-value is the odds you'd see a result this extreme if nothing real were actually going on.
cards.a: A p-value estimates the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming there's actually no real effect. The smaller the p-value, the less likely that outcome is to be pure chance — below 0.05 is the common cutoff, which is why it's the usual bar for calling a client's test result “statistically significant” rather than noise.

cards.q: What is a confidence interval?
cards.takeaway: A confidence interval is a range of plausible values, not a single guess — it expresses how much uncertainty surrounds an estimate.
cards.a: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for something you don't know exactly — like a population average — built from your sample data, rather than one single point estimate. A 95% confidence interval means that if you repeated the same sampling process many times, about 95% of the intervals you'd construct would contain the true value. It's a way of expressing uncertainty around an estimate — useful shorthand when you need to tell a client how much to trust a number, not a guarantee about any one specific interval.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co. wants to know how much of NorthPeak Airlines' recent revenue uptick came from its new marketing campaign versus other factors, like added routes or seasonal demand. What tool would you reach for, and what would it tell the client?
cards.takeaway: Regression puts a number on how much an outcome changes when an input changes.
cards.a: This is a regression problem: it estimates the relationship between an outcome (revenue) and the factors that might explain it (marketing spend, route count, seasonality), letting you put a number on how much revenue shifts as each input changes while holding the others constant. That's exactly the kind of question regression is built for in a business setting — forecasting sales, isolating what marketing spend or pricing actually does to revenue, and ranking which factors matter most.

cards.takeaway: A/B testing randomly splits an audience into two groups to fairly compare which version performs better.

cards.q: A client's product team surveys only its loyalty-program members about a new subscription tier and reports 90% approval. Your case team should flag this before it goes in the client's board deck — why?
cards.takeaway: Sample bias means your data doesn't represent the population you're trying to understand, so conclusions don't generalize.
cards.a: That 90% is sample bias in action: loyalty-program members aren't representative of the broader customer base the client is trying to understand, so the result won't generalize. It's the classic version of surveying only your existing customers about a new idea — you'd completely miss the opinions of everyone who looked at what you offer and decided not to buy, which is often exactly the group a new subscription tier needs to win over.

cards.q: What’s the difference between descriptive and predictive analytics?
cards.takeaway: Descriptive analytics explains what already happened; predictive analytics forecasts what's likely to happen next.
cards.a: Descriptive analytics summarizes what has already happened — like last quarter's sales broken out by region. Predictive analytics goes further, using patterns in that historical data to estimate what's likely to happen next, like forecasting next quarter's numbers. Most case analysis starts descriptive, establishing a clear picture of what happened, before it moves on to predicting or recommending what to do next.

name: Management & Strategy Frameworks
description: The core frameworks used to analyze markets, competitors, and business decisions.
intro: Case interviews and strategy conversations lean heavily on a small set of well-known frameworks, SWOT, Porter’s five forces, the kind of tools that give structure to a messy business question. This deck introduces each one from scratch: what it is for, when it actually applies, and the trap of using it as a checklist instead of a thinking tool. If you have never used a strategy framework before, this is designed to get you comfortable enough to reach for the right one under pressure.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group, a mid-size apparel chain, is trying to decide whether to expand into a new region. Before the team builds a recommendation, the engagement manager asks you to lay out where the client stands today. What framework do you reach for?
cards.takeaway: SWOT sorts a company's position into internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.
cards.a: Start with a SWOT analysis, a simple four-box way to take stock of where a company stands before making a strategic call. Strengths and weaknesses are internal, things the client controls, like its brand or cost structure, while opportunities and threats come from the external environment, like market trends or new competitors. Laying all four out side by side helps the team surface what to build on, what to fix, what to chase, and what to defend against, before proposing any recommendation to expand.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co. is considering entering the packaged foods industry and has hired your firm to assess whether it's an attractive market to enter. What framework would you use to size up industry attractiveness, and what does it look at?
cards.takeaway: Five surrounding pressures, rivals, entrants, substitutes, and supplier/buyer power, decide how profitable an industry can be.

If most of these forces are strong, they squeeze margins and make the industry a tougher place to make money; if they're weak, incumbents tend to enjoy healthier profits, a call the team needs to make before recommending Bramwell enter.

cards.q: What does “economies of scale” mean?
cards.takeaway: Average cost per unit drops as production volume rises, letting big companies price lower.
cards.a: Economies of scale is the tendency for a company's average cost per unit to fall as it produces more, a lever worth flagging any time a client's advantage rests on scale. Fixed costs, like a factory or corporate overhead, get spread across a larger number of units, and higher volumes often let a company negotiate better prices from suppliers too. It's a big reason large incumbents can often compete on price in ways smaller rivals simply can't afford to match.

cards.q: What is opportunity cost?
cards.takeaway: Opportunity cost is what you give up by not choosing the next-best alternative.
cards.a: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option you give up when you make a choice. It matters in case interviews and real strategy work alike because the true cost of any decision isn't just the money spent on it, it's also whatever else that same time, money, or resource could have produced instead.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a company’s mission and its strategy?
cards.takeaway: Mission is why a company exists; strategy is how it competes to get there.
cards.a: A mission statement explains why an organization exists and what it's fundamentally trying to achieve, while strategy is the specific plan for how it will compete and allocate resources to accomplish that. Mission tends to stay fixed for years or decades, while strategy adapts as markets, competitors, and client priorities change.

cards.q: Denholm Coffee Roasters, a client of your firm, is weighing whether to buy its own bean farms and also open branded retail cafes. What strategic move is this, and how would you frame the options for the client?
cards.takeaway: Vertical integration means owning more of your own supply chain, upstream or downstream.
cards.a: This is vertical integration, taking ownership of additional stages of your own supply chain. Backward integration would mean Denholm acquiring bean farms, moving upstream toward raw materials; forward integration would mean opening its own retail cafes, moving downstream toward the customer. Clients pursue it to control costs, secure supply, or capture margin that would otherwise go to an outside partner, though each direction comes with its own execution risk worth flagging.

cards.q: Aldercrest Furniture, a mid-market retailer, asks your team how it should compete against both big-box discounters and boutique design brands. What are Michael Porter's three generic strategies for building a competitive advantage, and how might you frame Aldercrest's choice?

cards.a: A competitive advantage is something that lets a company consistently outperform its rivals over time. Porter described three generic strategies for building one: cost leadership, becoming the lowest-cost producer and competing on price; differentiation, offering something distinctly better that customers will pay a premium for; and focus, applying either of those approaches to a narrow market segment instead of the whole industry. For Aldercrest, the team would need to help the client pick a lane rather than get stuck in the middle, competing against discounters on price while boutique brands out-differentiate them.

cards.q: What does “economies of scope” mean, and how is it different from economies of scale?
cards.takeaway: Economies of scope save money by producing different products together, not just more of one.
cards.a: Economies of scope are cost savings a company gets from producing multiple related products together rather than separately, for example by sharing R&D, distribution, or manufacturing capacity across product lines. It's a different lever from economies of scale, which comes from producing more of the same thing rather than a wider mix of things, worth distinguishing clearly if a case turns on which one is actually driving a client's costs.

name: Case Interview Structuring
description: How to build, communicate, and adapt a live case structure under interview pressure, not just which frameworks to memorize.
intro: Case interviews aren't won by memorizing a list of frameworks, they're won by how you structure, communicate, and adapt your thinking live, in real time, in front of an interviewer. This deck focuses on the process itself: breaking a broad prompt into a MECE issue tree, framing your structure out loud in the first few minutes, leading with a hypothesis instead of exploring everything equally, and recovering cleanly when new information proves your first structure wrong. If you already know your frameworks and want to sharpen how you actually run a case, this is built for that.

cards.q: What does MECE actually mean, and why does it matter for how you structure a case?
cards.takeaway: MECE means your buckets don't overlap and together cover the whole problem, so nothing's double-counted or missing.
cards.a: MECE stands for mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive: each branch of your structure shouldn't overlap with another, and together the branches should cover the entire problem. In a case, that keeps you from counting the same driver twice under two different buckets, and from leaving an entire category of the problem unexamined. The practical test isn't reciting the acronym, it's asking yourself, before you speak, whether a given fact could plausibly belong to two of your buckets at once, or whether there's a whole area your structure doesn't touch. Real interview structures are rarely perfectly MECE, but they should be close enough that the interviewer never has to ask "where would that go?"

cards.q: NorthPeak Airlines, a regional airline, comes to you because profits fell 20% last year and the CEO wants to know why. How do you build an issue tree to break that question down?
cards.takeaway: Split the driving question into MECE branches, then keep splitting until each branch is a fact you could go verify.
cards.a: Start with the driving question at the top of the page, why did NorthPeak's profit fall 20%, and split it into its first MECE layer: since profit equals revenue minus cost, one branch is revenue and the other is cost. Each branch then splits again, revenue into price and volume, cost into fixed and variable, and volume can split further into individual routes or ticket classes if that's where the real story lives. Keep branching until each end node is something you could actually go check with a number, like "average fare on the Denver-Boise route," not a vague theme like "market conditions." The finished tree becomes your map for deciding which branches are worth digging into first, not just a diagram you draw and set aside.

cards.q: What's the essential difference between a profitability case and a market-entry case, and how does it change the driving question you're answering?
cards.takeaway: Profitability cases diagnose why a number moved; market-entry cases decide whether to make a move at all.
cards.a: A profitability case starts from a problem that's already happened, profit or margin has moved in the wrong direction, and the driving question is diagnostic: which specific lever, price, volume, fixed cost, or variable cost, actually caused the change, and what should the client do about it. A market-entry case starts from a decision the client hasn't made yet, whether to enter a new market, launch a product, or make an acquisition, and the driving question is evaluative: is this worth doing, compared to the alternative of not doing it. That distinction should reshape your structure, not just your opening line: a profitability tree branches through revenue and cost hunting for the delta, while a market-entry tree branches through market attractiveness, the client's ability to win in it, and the financial return, because you're building a case for or against a decision rather than diagnosing what already broke.

cards.q: You've just heard the prompt and taken your silent structuring time. How should you actually lay out and walk the interviewer through your structure in the next few minutes?
cards.takeaway: State the objective, name your buckets top-down, then say which branch you'd start with and why.
cards.a: Open by restating the objective in your own words so the interviewer knows you understood the question, then walk through your structure top-down: name the two or three main buckets before diving into any sub-branch, so the interviewer can follow the shape of your thinking before the detail. Say each bucket out loud as a short label, not a paragraph, drawing it on paper as you talk if you have one in front of you. Close by telling the interviewer which branch you'd want to start with and why, since a structure that never turns into a starting point is just a list. The whole moment should take well under two minutes, structure is meant to set up the conversation, not replace it.

cards.q: What's the difference between reciting a memorized framework and building a structure live for the prompt in front of you, and why can interviewers usually tell?
cards.takeaway: A memorized framework ignores the specific prompt; a live structure is built from the actual facts you were given.
cards.a: A scripted framework is a generic template, the classic profitability tree or 4Ps, recited the same way regardless of what the prompt actually said, and it shows up as buckets that don't quite fit: a market-entry structure applied to a cost problem, or category names that don't match the client in the prompt. A structure built live starts from the specific facts and objective you were just given and only borrows the shape of a familiar framework where it genuinely applies, which is why it sounds tailored, using the client's actual situation, numbers, and constraints instead of generic labels. Interviewers can tell the difference almost immediately because a scripted structure tends to arrive too fast, sound identical to the last several candidates, and fall apart the moment a follow-up question pushes on a branch that doesn't actually apply here. The fix isn't memorizing more frameworks, it's practicing the underlying skill, breaking a novel question into MECE parts, so you can build the right structure for whatever prompt shows up.

cards.q: You've spent 25 minutes working through Ferrow Retail Group's declining store profitability and found the real driver is rising labor cost at a handful of underperforming stores, not weak sales. How do you wrap up the case?
cards.takeaway: Lead with the recommendation, back it with your top two or three findings, then flag the key risk.
cards.a: Synthesis means answering the original question directly, not narrating everything you did to get there, so lead with the recommendation itself: Ferrow should address labor cost at the specific underperforming stores rather than launch a broad sales initiative. Back it up with the two or three findings that actually drove that answer, in this case that labor cost per store rose faster than revenue at a specific subset of locations while sales held roughly flat elsewhere, skipping the dead ends you explored along the way. Name the biggest risk or open question, for example whether the labor cost spike is a one-off staffing issue or a structural wage trend, and what you'd want to check next to be sure. A good close takes well under a minute and could stand alone as the answer, even if the interviewer heard nothing else you said.

cards.q: Fifteen minutes into a case for Bramwell & Co., new data makes it clear your original structure is aimed at the wrong problem. What do you do?
cards.takeaway: Name the mismatch out loud, adjust the structure on the spot, and keep going, don't pretend nothing changed.
cards.a: The worst move is plowing ahead on a structure you already know doesn't fit, or quietly abandoning it without saying anything, both leave the interviewer unsure whether you've noticed the problem at all. Instead, name it directly: "this new data suggests the issue is really about X, not Y, let me adjust my structure," then briefly restate the one or two branches that change. You don't need to rebuild the whole tree from scratch, usually only the branch that's now wrong needs to move, the rest of your structure often still holds. Interviewers read a clean recovery as a strong signal, real client work is full of information that overturns your first hypothesis, and handling it calmly is closer to the actual job than never being wrong in the first place.

cards.q: What does it mean to be "hypothesis-driven" in a case, and how is it different from just working through your structure branch by branch in order?
cards.takeaway: Lead with your best guess at the answer, then test it first, instead of exploring every branch equally.
cards.a: Being hypothesis-driven means forming an early, informed guess about what the answer probably is, based on the prompt and the first facts you're given, and then using your structure to go test that guess first rather than working through every branch in the order you listed them. It's different from exhaustive branch-by-branch exploration, which treats every part of the tree as equally likely to hold the answer and burns limited case time confirming things that were never really in question. A hypothesis isn't a guess you're married to, if the data doesn't support it, you drop it and form a new one, but leading with one gives you a reason to ask for the data that actually matters instead of every data point available. It mirrors how real consulting engagements run: you rarely have time to check everything, so you prioritize based on what's most likely to be true and most valuable to confirm.

cards.q: Halverson Industries is losing money on its core manufacturing business and separately weighing whether to enter a new overseas market. How do you build a structure that handles both a profitability problem and a market-entry decision in the same case?
cards.takeaway: Treat it as two connected trees: diagnose the core problem first, then use that answer to inform the entry decision.
cards.a: Resist the urge to mash both prompts into one tree, build two separate MECE structures, a profitability tree for the manufacturing decline and a market-entry tree for the overseas decision, and connect them explicitly rather than blending their branches together. Sequence matters: diagnosing the core profitability problem first usually matters more, since a company bleeding cash domestically has a weaker case for funding an expansion, and what you learn there, for instance whether the problem is temporary or structural, directly changes how attractive the new market decision looks. State that sequencing out loud to the interviewer before you start, for example "I'd want to understand the manufacturing issue first, since it affects how much capacity Halverson has to fund entering a new market," so the connection between the two trees is clear rather than left implicit. The goal isn't a single unified diagram, it's showing you can hold two structures in mind at once and reason about how the answer to one changes the other.

name: Market Sizing & Guesstimates
description: How to structure a defensible estimate under uncertainty when an interviewer asks you to size something with no data given.
intro: Market sizing questions, how many piano tuners are in a city, how big is the market for a new product, are a consulting-interview staple precisely because there's no dataset to recall, only a structure to build live. This deck breaks down the toolkit: top-down versus bottom-up thinking, clean population segmentation, sanity-checking your own numbers, and the habits that separate a defensible estimate from a guess. Work through it and the next guesstimate question won't feel like a trick, it'll feel like a format you already know.

cards.q: When an interviewer asks you to estimate something like the number of piano tuners in a city, what are they actually evaluating?
cards.takeaway: They're grading your structure and logic under uncertainty, not whether you nail the exact number.
cards.a: Market sizing questions test whether you can build a clear, logical structure to estimate an unknown quantity when you don't have the data memorized. Interviewers care about how you break the problem down, state your assumptions out loud, and adjust when something seems off, not whether your final number matches a figure sitting in a database somewhere. A well-reasoned estimate that lands in a plausible range beats a lucky guess with no visible logic every time. The real skill being tested is comfort with ambiguity, can you make steady progress on a problem that hands you no clean, given inputs.

cards.q: What's the difference between a top-down and a bottom-up approach to market sizing, and when should you use each?
cards.takeaway: Top-down starts from a big number and narrows it down; bottom-up builds the estimate up from a single unit.
cards.a: A top-down approach starts with a large, known or estimable figure, like a country's population, and narrows it step by step by applying percentages until you reach the answer. A bottom-up approach does the opposite, it starts from a small, concrete unit, like one store's average daily customers, and multiplies up to the whole market. Top-down tends to work well when you have a solid anchor number to start from, while bottom-up is often more defensible when the top-line figure is fuzzy but a single unit of the business is easy to picture. Strong answers sometimes use both directions on the same question, as a way of cross-checking that the two paths land in the same neighborhood.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail's interviewer asks you to estimate how many people in Corvale, a fictional city of 900,000, buy a birthday cake in a given year. How do you segment the population without double-counting or leaving gaps?
cards.takeaway: Split the population into buckets that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, no overlaps, no gaps.
cards.a: The core discipline is MECE: every person in Corvale should fall into exactly one segment, and every segment together should cover the whole population. For a birthday-cake question, splitting by age band, say under 10, 10 to 64, and 65-plus, works cleanly because everyone has exactly one age; splitting by categories like 'families' and 'young professionals' instead risks double-counting a young professional who is also a parent. Once the segments are clean, you can apply a different purchase-rate assumption to each, for instance a different bakery-purchase rate for a young child's party versus an adult birthday, and add the pieces back up knowing nothing was counted twice or missed entirely.

cards.q: Partway through an estimate you land on a number, say 40,000 hospital beds in Aldmere, a fictional mid-size country. How do you sanity-check that against something you already know?
cards.takeaway: Convert your estimate to a per-capita rate and compare it to a number you already trust.
cards.a: Raw totals are hard to judge, but rates are easy to sanity check. Take your estimate, divide it by population to get something like 'beds per 1,000 people,' and compare that to a rough figure you're confident is roughly right, such as knowing developed countries generally sit somewhere around two to four hospital beds per 1,000 people. If your derived rate is wildly outside that plausible range, some step upstream is probably off, and it's far easier to catch that with a familiar per-capita ratio than by staring at a seven-digit total. This kind of check is also worth narrating out loud, since it shows the interviewer you're pressure-testing your own math rather than trusting it blindly.

cards.q: As you work through a multi-step estimate, how should you handle rounding along the way?
cards.takeaway: Round to clean numbers on purpose, say it out loud, and track which direction each round pushes your answer.
cards.a: Pick simple, round inputs at each step, for example treating a population of 4.3 million as 4 million, and state clearly that you're doing it. This keeps your mental math fast and keeps the interviewer able to follow your logic in real time instead of getting lost in decimals. It also helps to notice whether you're consistently rounding up or down across several steps; if most of your rounds went down to make the math easy, your final number is probably a slight underestimate, and flagging that directly reads as more rigorous than presenting a rounded chain of assumptions as if it were precise.

cards.q: Walk through how you'd structure an estimate for the number of independent coffee shops in Dunmoor, a fictional mid-size city of 500,000 people.
cards.takeaway: Anchor on population, narrow to regular buyers, then divide by what one shop can realistically serve.
cards.a: Start from Dunmoor's population of 500,000 and estimate the share who buy coffee from a shop a few times a week or more, say 30%, giving roughly 150,000 regular customers. Next estimate how often each of them visits per week, maybe 3 times, and what fraction of those visits go to an independent shop rather than a chain, say half, which works out to about 225,000 independent-shop visits per week. Finally, estimate how many customers one independent shop can realistically serve in a week, perhaps 1,500, and divide, 225,000 divided by 1,500 lands you at roughly 150 independent coffee shops in Dunmoor. Each step used one clean, stated assumption, which is exactly what makes the answer defensible even though none of the inputs were 'known' facts.

cards.q: An interviewer asks you to estimate the number of accordion repair technicians in Velmara, a small fictional country you know almost nothing about. What do you do when you have no anchor data at all?
cards.takeaway: When you lack a direct anchor, build one from a related number you're more confident estimating.
cards.a: Start with whatever you're most confident about, usually total population, then work through a chain of plausible ratios to get closer to the target: how many households might own an accordion, how often an owned instrument needs professional repair, and how many repairs one technician can realistically handle in a year. Say each assumption out loud and flag which ones you're least sure of, since the interviewer usually cares more about watching you reason through genuine uncertainty than about a lucky guess. It's also completely fair to state a reasonable working assumption about Velmara, like an approximate population, if the interviewer hasn't given you one, that's a normal, expected part of the exercise, not a sign that you're stuck.

cards.q: A candidate estimates that Bramwell Fitness's target city has 1.2 million gym memberships in a population of 400,000. What went wrong, and what other mistakes commonly wreck an estimate like this?
cards.takeaway: Watch for nesting errors, unstated assumptions, and any input that's implausible on its face.
cards.a: That example fails a basic plausibility check, it implies each person holds three memberships, which points to a nesting error, some rate probably got applied twice, or applied to the wrong base, like visits per week mistaken for total members. Other common breakdowns include quietly changing an assumption partway through without saying so, stacking several unstated guesses on top of each other until the interviewer can no longer follow the logic, and feeding in an input that's implausible on its own, like assuming 90% of adults belong to a gym. The fix for all of them is the same habit, say every assumption out loud as you make it, and pause to ask whether the resulting number still sounds like something that could be true in the real world.

cards.q: You've landed on a final number, say 60,000 gym memberships in Aldmere. What's the last thing you should do before giving that answer to the interviewer?
cards.takeaway: Zoom out and ask whether the number would surprise a reasonably informed adult, then explain why or adjust.
cards.a: Before saying the number out loud, translate it into something intuitive, like memberships per adult or per household, and ask yourself whether that rate feels plausible given everyday experience. It also helps to briefly restate the chain of assumptions that produced it, since walking back through the logic often surfaces one step that quietly went too high or too low. If the number still feels off, it's better to flag that honestly, something like 'this feels a bit high, and I think it's because of X,' than to present a suspicious number with total confidence, interviewers consistently rate that kind of self-awareness higher than a falsely confident wrong answer.

name: Accounting Fundamentals
description: Debits, credits, and how the books actually get built.
intro: Accounting is the record-keeping system behind every financial statement, and understanding it, even at a basic level, makes everything else in finance click into place faster. This deck starts from the actual mechanics: what double-entry bookkeeping means, how debits and credits work, and how the books get built up from a single transaction. It is written for someone who has never taken an accounting class, not as a shortcut around learning it, but as a clear first pass.

cards.q: What is double-entry bookkeeping?
cards.takeaway: Every transaction hits two accounts of equal value, so the books always stay in balance.
cards.a: Every transaction gets recorded twice, once as a debit and once as a credit, always for the same amount. That's what keeps the accounting equation, Assets = Liabilities + Equity, in balance no matter how many transactions pile up. It also builds in a natural error check: if total debits and credits ever stop matching, you know something was recorded wrong somewhere — the same logic that has to hold in every model you'll ever build off a company's books.

cards.q: What do “debit” and “credit” actually mean in accounting?
cards.takeaway: Debit means left, credit means right — which one grows an account depends on the account type.
cards.a: Debit and credit aren't inherently "increase" or "decrease" — they just mean the left and right side of an account. What each one does depends on the account type: debits increase assets and expenses (and decrease liabilities, equity, and revenue), while credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue (and decrease assets and expenses). Memorize which accounts move which way, and the rest of double-entry bookkeeping follows from that.

cards.q: What is a T-account?
cards.takeaway: A T-account is a quick sketch of one account: debits on the left, credits on the right.

cards.q: What is the difference between a journal entry and the general ledger?
cards.takeaway: Journal entries record transactions in order; the ledger re-sorts them by account.
cards.a: A journal entry is the raw, chronological record of a transaction: it shows exactly which accounts were debited and credited as the transaction happened. The general ledger then reorganizes those entries by account, pulling every transaction that touched "Cash" or "Revenue," for example, into one place so you can track that account's running balance. Think of the journal as the diary and the ledger as the filing system built from it — the distinction that matters when you're handed a target's books and need to trace a number back to the transaction that created it.

cards.q: You're on the deal team for Kessler Industrial's sale process, and the seller's controller hands your group Q3 financials that haven't been closed out yet. Before the numbers go into the model, your VP wants to know: what is an adjusting entry, and why is it needed at the end of a period?
cards.takeaway: Adjusting entries true up the books so revenue and expenses land in the right period.
cards.a: An adjusting entry updates account balances at the end of a period to capture revenue that's been earned, or an expense that's been incurred, but hasn't been recorded yet — think accrued interest, or a prepaid expense that's now been used up. They're needed because plenty of transactions span multiple periods, and without them, revenue and expenses would land in the wrong period and distort the financial statements. In a deal context that's not academic: financials handed over mid-period, like the ones Kessler's controller just sent, need these entries booked before you can trust them enough to build a model on top of.

cards.q: Your team is comparing Ferrow Retail against a public comp for a pitch book, and Ferrow uses LIFO while the comp uses FIFO. Before the margins can be compared apples-to-apples, your VP wants a quick explanation: what’s the difference between FIFO and LIFO inventory valuation?
cards.takeaway: FIFO sells your oldest inventory first; LIFO sells the newest — and rising prices make the choice matter.
cards.a: FIFO (first in, first out) assumes the oldest units in inventory get sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects older, typically cheaper, costs. LIFO (last in, first out) assumes the newest units get sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects more recent, typically higher, costs. When prices are rising, that difference shows up on the financials: FIFO tends to report higher profit and a higher inventory value, while LIFO reports lower profit but a smaller tax bill. That's exactly why you can't line up Ferrow's margins against a FIFO comp without adjusting for the accounting difference first.

cards.q: You're building the base-case LBO model for the Thornfield Manufacturing deal, and your associate wants a simple capex and depreciation schedule rather than something modeled asset-by-asset. What is depreciation, and why is straight-line depreciation the simplest method?
cards.takeaway: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life instead of expensing it all at once.
cards.a: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset, like equipment or a building, across its useful life instead of expensing the full purchase price the year it's bought, matching the expense to the years the asset actually helps generate revenue. Straight-line depreciation is the simplest version: it expenses an equal amount every year, which makes it easy to calculate and forecast, even though many assets really lose value faster in their early years than a straight line implies. That simplicity is exactly why it's the default assumption in a base-case model unless there's a specific reason to build something more granular.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a contra account and a regular account?
cards.takeaway: A contra account runs opposite its partner account, shrinking it instead of growing it.
cards.a: A regular account moves in its natural direction — assets and expenses grow with debits, for example. A contra account is paired with a related account but moves in the opposite direction, reducing that account's reported balance instead of adding to it. Accumulated depreciation is the classic example: paired with a fixed asset account, it carries a credit balance and lowers the asset's book value on the balance sheet — the exact line you'll be linking to a depreciation schedule when you build out a model's balance sheet.

cards.q: During diligence on the Halstead Foods acquisition, you notice the target capitalized a cost that arguably should have been expensed, flattering reported EBITDA. Before flagging it to your MD, make sure you can explain: what is the difference between capitalizing a cost and expensing it?
cards.takeaway: Capitalize a cost if its value lasts years; expense it if the benefit ends this period.
cards.a: Capitalizing a cost means recording it as an asset on the balance sheet and spreading it over time through depreciation or amortization, because it creates value beyond the current period — buying equipment, for instance. Expensing a cost means recording the full amount immediately on the income statement, because the benefit is used up in the current period, like office supplies. The choice affects both the balance sheet and how quickly a cost hits reported profit — and it's a classic spot for quality-of-earnings adjustments in diligence, since capitalizing a cost that should have been expensed makes near-term EBITDA look better than it really is.

name: Financial Markets & Instruments
description: How stocks, bonds, and other instruments actually trade.
intro: This deck covers how stocks, bonds, and other financial instruments actually trade, the difference between where a security is first issued and where it changes hands afterward, and the basic mechanics behind the markets you hear about in the news. It is aimed at giving you enough grounding to talk about markets confidently in an interview, not at making you a trader. No assumed background beyond general curiosity about how finance works.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a primary market and a secondary market?
cards.takeaway: Primary market money goes to the company; secondary market money just moves between investors.
cards.a: In the primary market, a company sells brand-new securities directly to investors for the first time, an IPO being the classic example, and the company keeps the proceeds — this is the deal-side work an ECM (equity capital markets) team executes. In the secondary market, investors simply trade those already-issued securities amongst themselves, like on the NYSE or Nasdaq, and the issuing company isn't even a party to the transaction. Only the primary market actually raises new capital for the company; the secondary market just lets ownership change hands.

cards.q: Your group is staffed on the IPO for Ferrow Retail Group, a private-equity-backed retailer. Before the kickoff call, a first-year analyst asks you: what is an IPO, exactly?
cards.takeaway: An IPO is a private company's first sale of shares to the public, becoming publicly traded.
cards.a: An IPO, or initial public offering, is the process by which a private company like Ferrow Retail sells shares to the public for the first time and becomes a publicly traded company. It lets the company raise capital from a much broader pool of investors, but in exchange, existing owners give up some ownership and the company takes on the disclosure and reporting obligations that come with being public.

cards.q: You're on the DCM team pricing a new bond for Bramwell & Co. Overnight the bond's price drops, and a client asks why the yield just moved — how do you explain the relationship between a bond's yield and its price?
cards.takeaway: A bond's yield and price always move in opposite directions.
cards.a: A bond's yield is the return an investor actually earns from holding it, and it moves inversely to the bond's price: when price falls, like it just did on Bramwell's bond, yield rises, because the same fixed coupon payments now represent a bigger percentage return on the lower price paid. Pay less for the same future cash flows and your return goes up; pay more and it goes down. This inverse relationship is one of the most fundamental mechanics in fixed income markets.

cards.takeaway: Lower credit rating means higher default risk, so investors demand a higher yield.

Because risk and return are linked, a rating this low means Bramwell will have to offer a higher yield to compensate investors for taking on that extra default risk.

cards.q: What is the bid-ask spread?
cards.takeaway: The bid-ask spread is the gap between what buyers offer and what sellers demand.
cards.a: The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a security, and the ask is the lowest price a seller is willing to accept; the difference between the two is the spread a trading desk watches all day. A narrow spread usually signals a liquid market with plenty of active buyers and sellers, while a wide spread signals lower liquidity or more uncertainty about fair value.

cards.q: What is a market maker?
cards.takeaway: Market makers quote both sides of the market constantly, earning the spread instead of betting on price direction.
cards.a: A market maker is a firm that continuously quotes both a bid and an ask price for a security, standing ready to buy or sell at those prices at any time — it's the kind of two-sided flow you'd see running through a bank's trading desk. That constant two-sided quoting is what supplies liquidity to the market. Their profit comes from capturing the bid-ask spread across that flow of trades, not from predicting which way the price will move.

cards.q: What is a derivative, and what are options and futures examples of?
cards.takeaway: A derivative's value comes from something else entirely; options and futures are the two classic examples.
cards.a: A derivative is a financial contract with no value of its own; its value is derived from an underlying asset, like a stock, commodity, or index — the kind of exposure a derivatives or structuring desk trades all day. Options and futures are both derivatives, but they work differently: an option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a set price, while a futures contract is an obligation, both sides are locked in to buy or sell it at a set price on a set future date.

cards.q: A hedge fund client, Talbrook Capital, wants to protect a long position in Ferrow Retail stock ahead of earnings. Your VP asks you to walk through the difference between a call option and a put option before the call.
cards.takeaway: Calls profit when the price rises above the strike; puts profit when it falls below it.
cards.a: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset, like Ferrow Retail stock, at a set strike price before expiration, and investors buy calls when they expect the price to rise. A put option gives the holder the right to sell at the strike price, which is the side Talbrook would look at to hedge against a drop, and investors buy puts when they expect the price to fall. Either way, it's a right, not an obligation, so the holder can just let the option expire worthless if exercising it wouldn't be profitable.

cards.takeaway: Market cap is share price times shares outstanding, a company's total public equity value.

name: Microeconomics & Market Structures
description: Supply, demand, and how competition shapes a market.
intro: Interviewers in business, strategy, and even product roles often lean on basic economic reasoning: supply and demand, how competition shapes pricing, what happens when a market has only a few players instead of many. This deck builds those ideas up from first principles, so if the words "market structure" currently mean nothing to you, that is exactly who this is for. The goal is to be able to reason through an economic scenario out loud, not recite a textbook definition.

cards.q: What does the law of demand state?
cards.takeaway: Higher prices mean people buy less; lower prices mean they buy more.
cards.a: The law of demand says that, all else equal, a higher price leads people to buy less of a good, and a lower price leads them to buy more, which is what gives the demand curve its downward slope. It happens because as something gets relatively more expensive, buyers shift toward substitutes that meet the same need for less — the same substitution logic that shows up whenever a case turns on a proposed price change.

cards.q: What is price elasticity of demand?
cards.takeaway: Elasticity measures how sharply quantity demanded reacts when price moves.
cards.a: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded changes when price changes. Demand is “elastic” when a small price move causes a big swing in quantity, typical for goods with close substitutes, and “inelastic” when quantity barely budges even as price changes a lot, typical for necessities with few substitutes. It's a fast gut-check in any pricing case: the more substitutes a product has, the less room there is to raise price without losing volume.

cards.q: What is equilibrium price?
cards.takeaway: Equilibrium is the one price where what buyers want to buy matches what sellers want to sell.
cards.a: Equilibrium price is the price where the quantity buyers want to purchase exactly matches the quantity sellers want to offer, so there’s no leftover surplus and no shortage. Graphically, it’s the point where the supply and demand curves cross, and real markets tend to drift toward this price naturally over time — useful as a baseline anytime a case asks you to reason about where a market's price should settle.
