cards.q: A private equity client is comparing two possible investments: one in an industry where hundreds of small farms sell an identical commodity grain, and one in an industry where a single firm, Bramwell & Co., owns the only patented process for a specialized industrial coating. How would you characterize each market structure, and what does that imply for pricing power?
cards.takeaway: Perfect competition has many price takers; a monopoly has one price setter.
cards.a: The grain market looks like perfect competition: many firms sell identical products and no single one is big enough to move the market price, so each just accepts, or “takes,” the going price. Bramwell & Co. looks like a monopoly: it is effectively the entire market for that coating, giving it real control over price, which typically means higher prices and less output than a competitive market would deliver — and, for the PE client, a very different pricing-power story.

cards.q: NorthPeak Airlines is one of four carriers controlling nearly all the traffic on a regional route. When NorthPeak cuts fares 10%, the other three match the cut within days. What market structure is this, and why does it produce that reactive behavior?
cards.takeaway: A few big firms dominate the market, and each one watches the others' every move.
cards.a: This is an oligopoly: a market controlled by a small number of large firms, where one firm’s decisions, on pricing especially, directly affect the others and usually provoke a response. Airlines are a classic real-world example of this dynamic — a handful of players control most of a route, so a fare cut by one carrier squeezes the others' volume enough that matching it is the safer move.

cards.q: The CEO of Bramwell & Co. asks you how many units of a new product line the company should manufacture to maximize profit. How would you use marginal cost and marginal revenue to find that point?
cards.takeaway: Keep producing while extra revenue beats extra cost; stop right where they meet.
cards.a: Marginal cost is what it costs Bramwell to produce one more unit, and marginal revenue is what that extra unit brings in. The profit-maximizing move is to keep producing as long as marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, and stop right at the point where the two are equal, since pushing past that point would only shrink total profit.

cards.q: A client is weighing whether to enter the industrial water-filtration market, currently held by three incumbents with long-standing patents and multi-year supplier contracts. What would you tell them about barriers to entry here, and how should that shape their entry strategy?
cards.takeaway: Barriers to entry are whatever keeps new competitors from entering and challenging incumbents.
cards.a: A barrier to entry is anything that makes it hard for a new firm to break into a market and compete with the companies already there — think high startup costs, patents, strong brand loyalty, or economies of scale that let incumbents produce more cheaply than a newcomer could. Here, the patents and locked-in supplier contracts are both real barriers, so the client should expect a slow, capital-intensive entry, or consider a partnership or acquisition instead of competing head-on from day one.

cards.q: What is consumer surplus?
cards.takeaway: Consumer surplus is the extra value buyers get for paying less than they'd have accepted.
cards.a: Consumer surplus is the gap between what consumers were willing to pay for a good and what they actually paid, added up across every buyer in the market. It represents the bonus value consumers walk away with, and on a graph, it’s the area between the demand curve and the market price line — worth having on hand whenever a case asks you to weigh a pricing decision's impact on customers, not just on the firm.

name: Marketing Fundamentals
description: The core concepts behind how products get positioned and sold.
intro: Marketing questions show up in more interviews than people expect, not just marketing roles, but general business and case interviews that touch product or strategy. This deck covers the core vocabulary and frameworks, like the four Ps, that give you a structured way to talk about how a product actually gets positioned, priced, and sold. Written for someone starting from zero, with an emphasis on frameworks you can actually apply to a real example on the spot.

cards.q: Your client, Ferrow Retail Group, is about to launch a new private-label snack line and wants a structured way to plan the launch. What framework would you reach for, and what does it cover?
cards.takeaway: The 4 Ps are the four levers a company pulls to bring a product to market.
cards.a: Reach for the 4 Ps, or marketing mix: Product (what you're selling), Price (what it costs), Place (where and how customers can get it), and Promotion (how you tell people about it). For Ferrow's snack launch, that means nailing down what the product actually is, what it's priced at, which shelves or channels it lands in, and how shoppers hear about it. Every go-to-market decision falls under one of these four buckets, and getting them working together is what makes a launch land instead of falling flat.

cards.q: Bramwell & Co., a regional eyewear retailer, is expanding into a new market and isn't sure which customers to go after first or how to stand out once it's there. What three-step process would you walk the client through?
cards.takeaway: STP walks you from a broad, messy market down to one clear position in customers' minds.
cards.a: Walk Bramwell through STP: Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning. Segmentation splits the new market into groups that share similar needs, targeting picks which of those groups is actually worth pursuing first, and positioning defines how Bramwell should be perceived, relative to competitors, in that group's mind. Run through in order, it takes the client from 'everyone in this new market' to a specific, ownable position for a specific audience.

cards.q: What is brand equity, and why does it matter in a pricing engagement?
cards.takeaway: Brand equity is the extra value a name adds on top of what the product actually does.
cards.a: Brand equity is the value a brand name adds beyond the product's raw functional benefits: the premium customers will pay, the loyalty they show, and the trust they extend before they've even used it. It's often the first thing to check when a client's product and a competitor's are functionally identical but priced far apart — two nearly identical products can sell at very different prices purely because one has a name behind it that people already believe in.

cards.q: Larkspur Meals, a subscription meal-kit service, wants to know how much it can afford to spend acquiring a new subscriber and still turn a profit. What number would you calculate, and what does it capture?
cards.takeaway: CLV is the total profit one customer is worth over the whole relationship, not just their first order.
cards.a: Calculate customer lifetime value: the total revenue or profit Larkspur can expect from a single subscriber across the entire relationship, not just their first box. Because it captures repeat purchases over time, CLV is the number that tells Larkspur how much it can afford to spend acquiring a new customer and still come out ahead.

cards.q: What does AIDA stand for, and what is it used for?
cards.takeaway: AIDA maps the four stages a stranger passes through on the way to becoming a buyer.
cards.a: AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action, the stages a customer moves through before they buy: first they have to notice something exists, then care enough to learn more, then want it specifically, then actually act. Marketing teams, and anyone advising them on a campaign, use it as a checklist, making sure each piece of content moves people to the next stage instead of skipping ahead.

cards.q: What is market segmentation, and what are some common bases for it?
cards.takeaway: Segmentation splits one big, messy market into smaller groups that actually behave the same way.
cards.a: Market segmentation is the process of breaking a broad customer base into smaller groups that share similar characteristics or needs, so a company, or the team advising it, can market to each group more precisely than it could to everyone at once. Common bases include demographic (age, income), geographic (location), psychographic (lifestyle, values), and behavioral (purchase habits, brand loyalty).

cards.q: What's the difference between B2B and B2C marketing?
cards.takeaway: B2B sells to a committee on ROI; B2C sells to one person on emotion and price.
cards.a: B2B (business-to-business) marketing sells to other companies, where multiple stakeholders typically weigh in and decisions hinge on ROI over a longer sales cycle — the kind of buying committee you'd map out on a client engagement. B2C (business-to-consumer) marketing sells directly to individual consumers, where decisions are usually faster and driven more by emotion and price than by a formal evaluation process.

cards.q: What is a value proposition?
cards.takeaway: A value proposition is the one-line answer to 'why should I buy this instead of anything else?'
cards.a: A value proposition is a clear statement of the specific benefit a product delivers to its target customer, and why that beats the alternatives available to them. It's usually the first thing worth pressure-testing on an engagement — it exists to answer the customer's unspoken question up front: why choose this over everything else competing for their attention and money?

cards.q: Solenne Software's monthly revenue looks healthy and growing, but the CEO worries it's masking a deeper retention problem. What metric would you pull to check, and why can't total revenue alone tell you this?
cards.takeaway: Churn rate is the percentage of customers you're losing each period, the leak in the bucket.
cards.a: Pull churn rate: the share of customers who stop doing business with Solenne over a given period, a metric subscription businesses watch closely because it's their clearest signal of retention. A high churn rate means Solenne is losing customers faster than is sustainable, even while new signups make total revenue look fine on the surface — so growth and churn always have to be read together.

name: Operations & Supply Chain Management
description: How companies manage inventory, production, and the flow of goods.
intro: Operations questions test a different kind of thinking than finance ones: how a business actually moves inventory, manages production, and keeps a supply chain from breaking under pressure. This deck introduces the core concepts, like the bullwhip effect, through simple explanations first, building toward the vocabulary interviewers expect you to use fluently. No operations background needed, just a willingness to think about a business as a physical system, not just a spreadsheet.

cards.q: Ferrow Retail Group's category buyers see it every quarter: a small uptick in weekend foot traffic at stores turns into wildly swinging order quantities from their manufacturers a few weeks later. What's happening, and what's it called?
cards.takeaway: Small demand blips get amplified into big order swings the further upstream you look.
cards.a: This is the bullwhip effect: a small shift in real customer demand gets amplified as it passes upstream, from retailer to distributor to manufacturer, because each link tends to over-adjust its own orders instead of passing the true signal along unchanged. Those small overreactions stack at every step, so by the time the signal reaches Ferrow's manufacturers, a minor blip in weekend traffic looks like a huge swing in orders, distorting what's actually happening at the register.

cards.q: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management, and what's the tradeoff a case interviewer wants you to name?
cards.takeaway: JIT brings materials in only as production needs them, trading safety stock for leaner inventory.
cards.a: Just-in-time inventory management brings materials and components in right as production needs them, instead of stockpiling them in advance. That keeps holding costs and waste low, since there's little excess inventory sitting around. The tradeoff is fragility: with barely any buffer stock, a single disruption anywhere in the supply chain can quickly bring production to a halt. It's a favorite lever in operations cases: a client chasing the cost savings is also signing up for that exposure, and naming the tradeoff explicitly is what separates a strong answer from a list of definitions.

cards.q: What is Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), and why is it a useful reflex in an operations case?
cards.takeaway: EOQ finds the order size where ordering costs and holding costs balance out to the lowest total cost.
cards.a: Economic order quantity is the order size that minimizes total inventory cost, balancing two costs that pull in opposite directions: the fixed cost of placing an order, and the cost of storing the units once they've arrived. Order too little and you pay that fixed ordering cost too often; order too much and you pay more to store the excess. EOQ is simply the quantity where those two costs are lowest combined, which is why it's a handy structure to reach for whenever a case turns on 'how much should the client order at a time.'

cards.q: Bramwell & Co., a mid-sized furniture maker, is debating whether to keep building sofas against a demand forecast or switch to starting production only once a customer order comes in. What are the two production models on the table, and what's the tradeoff?
cards.takeaway: Push production guesses ahead of demand; pull production only makes what's already been ordered.
cards.a: Bramwell is weighing a push system, which produces to a forecast, building up inventory ahead of actual orders in the hope demand shows up to match it, against a pull system, which flips that logic: production only kicks off once a real customer order actually appears. Pull is the thinking behind JIT and cuts the risk of building sofas nobody ends up wanting, but it generally means longer wait times for the customer and less room to smooth production volume.

cards.q: What is Six Sigma, and how can its framework help structure a case answer?
cards.takeaway: Six Sigma hunts down process defects using data, aiming for near-flawless, 3.4-in-a-million quality.
cards.a: Six Sigma is a data-driven methodology for shrinking defects and variability in a process, aiming for a quality level where only about 3.4 defects occur per million opportunities. Teams typically work through it using DMAIC, a five-step cycle: Define the problem, Measure current performance, Analyze the root cause, Improve the process, and Control it so the gains stick. That same define-measure-analyze arc is a useful skeleton for walking an interviewer through any client process problem, not just a formal Six Sigma engagement.

cards.q: What is lead time, and why do interviewers ask about it in operations cases?
cards.takeaway: Lead time is the full clock from placing an order to actually having it in hand.
cards.a: Lead time is the total stretch between placing an order and actually receiving it, covering everything from processing and production to shipping. The shorter it is, the less safety stock a client needs to keep on hand to reliably meet customer demand, since there's less time for something to go wrong or for demand to shift in between. When a case involves a supplier switch or a new distribution route, lead time is usually the first number worth asking for.

cards.q: Your client, NorthPeak Manufacturing, is missing its quarterly output targets even though the plant manager insists the machines are running nearly non-stop. Before diving into the process itself, what metric would you check first, and what would it tell you?
cards.takeaway: Capacity utilization shows what share of a company's maximum output it's actually using.
cards.a: Start with capacity utilization: it measures how much of NorthPeak's total production capacity is actually being used, shown as a percentage of the maximum possible output. Low utilization can point to inefficiency or weak demand pulling orders away from the plant, while very high utilization is a warning sign too: the plant is close to its ceiling and at risk of bottlenecks if demand climbs any further. Either reading points you toward a different next question, which is exactly why it's worth checking before you go any deeper.

cards.q: What is safety stock, and why do companies hold it? What's the cost of holding too much?
cards.takeaway: Safety stock is the buffer inventory that absorbs surprise demand spikes or supply delays.
cards.a: Safety stock is extra inventory held beyond what's expected to be needed, acting as a cushion against uncertainty, like a sudden spike in orders or a delayed shipment. It lowers the risk of running out of stock, but it isn't free: it ties up capital and storage space, so companies weigh that cost against the protection it buys them. In a case, a client with chronic stockouts and a client with bloated warehouse costs can both trace back to the same lever, just tuned in opposite directions.

cards.q: At Dunmore Assembly Co.'s plant, three of four stations sit idle for stretches during the shift, yet the plant still can't hit its daily output target. Where should you start looking, and why?
cards.takeaway: A bottleneck is the slowest station in a process, and it caps what the whole system can produce.
cards.a: Start by finding Dunmore's bottleneck: the single stage in the process with the least capacity, which sets the ceiling on how much the entire line can produce no matter how efficient every other stage is. That's consistent with what the plant manager is describing, the idle stations are simply waiting on the slow one. Speeding up any other stage won't help, since output still can't exceed what the bottleneck allows, so improving the process starts with finding that constraint and fixing it first.
